primitives.name: Potentially Directed Path Definition
primitives.verbatim_quote: > **Definition 10 (potentially directed path).** In a PMG, a path p =〈V0,...,Vn〉 is said to be potentially directed (abbreviated as **p.d.**) fromV0to Vnif for every 0 _i n_ - 1, the edge between Viand _V_ i+1is not into Vior out of _V_ i+1.
primitives.latex: \text{Path } p = \langle V_0, ..., V_n \rangle \text{ is p.d. if } \forall i, \text{ edge } (V_i, V_{i+1}) \text{ is not into or out of } V_i \text{ or } V_{i+1}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'p': 'path in a partially directed graph', 'V₀...Vₙ': 'sequence of vertices', 'i': 'index in path'}
primitives.assumptions: Each edge in the path is neither incoming nor outgoing from its endpoints.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When any edge violates the condition, path is not potentially directed.

R5 resolves uncovered circle paths by making all edges undirected, assuming non-adjacency of endpoints. R10 handles conflicts when multiple paths lead to ambiguous orientations, resolving them based on adjacency of adjacent vertices. The definition of potentially directed paths ensures that orientations can be consistently applied without violating graph structure. These rules form a kernel of causal inference where each rule acts as a constraint on allowable edge directions, enabling robust identification of causal relationships in observational data. Failure modes occur when adjacency conditions are violated or when conflicting paths cannot be resolved due to shared vertices.
